content: Hydrocortisone and pramoxine topical formulations are used to alleviate inflammation and itching associated with corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. The medication should be applied to the affected area every 6 to 8 hours, depending on the severity of the condition. Topical corticosteroids, including hydrocortisone, may cause systemic effects, particularly when used with occlusive dressings, over large surface areas, or for prolonged periods. Occlusive dressings can be employed for conditions like psoriasis or recalcitrant dermatoses if necessary. Pramoxine, due to its unique chemical structure, has a lower risk of cross-sensitivity reactions in patients allergic to other local anesthetics. In pediatric patients, the use of this medication should be limited to the smallest effective amount to minimize the risk of systemic toxicity, as children may absorb higher amounts, leading to increased susceptibility to adverse effects. Common side effects of topical corticosteroids include burning, itching, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, hypertrichosis, acneiform eruptions, hypopigmentation, perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, skin maceration, secondary infections, skin atrophy, striae, and miliaria. Hypersensitivity to any component of the preparation is a contraindication. Systemic absorption of topical corticosteroids has been associated with reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression, manifestations of Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria. Factors that increase systemic absorption include the use of potent steroids, application over large areas, prolonged use, and the addition of occlusive dressings. Patients at risk for HPA axis suppression should be periodically evaluated using urinary free cortisol and ACTH stimulation tests. If suppression is detected, the drug should be withdrawn, the frequency of application reduced, or a less potent steroid substituted. Contact dermatitis may occur with use; if irritation develops, discontinue the medication and treat appropriately. Prolonged use may lead to fungal or bacterial superinfections; discontinue use if infections persist despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Topical corticosteroids may also cause Cushing’s syndrome, hyperglycemia, or glycosuria, particularly with occlusive dressings, application to denuded skin, large surface areas, or prolonged use. In elderly patients, the smallest effective dose should be used for the shortest duration possible. Aerosol containers should not be inserted directly into the anus. If no clinical or proctologic improvement is observed after 2 to 3 weeks, or if the condition worsens, discontinue use. During pregnancy, this medication is classified as Category C, meaning risk to the fetus cannot be ruled out. Its excretion in breast milk is unknown, so caution is advised during lactation. Hydrocortisone exerts anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive effects by suppressing the migration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and reversing increased capillary permeability. Pramoxine acts as a surface or local anesthetic. The extent of absorption is influenced by factors such as the vehicle, the integrity of the epidermal barrier, and the use of occlusive dressings. Protein binding is variable, and the drug is primarily metabolized by the liver and excreted in the urine. For formulary comparisons, adding plans allows users to evaluate the status of this drug relative to others in the same class. Formulary information may vary and is subject to change, so it is recommended to contact the applicable plan provider for the most current details.
